name: Dehydration cuts / water cutting

lead: Water cutting means deliberately losing body water, through water manipulation, sweating, sweat suits or saunas, to look drier and more defined for photos or events. It comes from weight-class sports such as combat sports and rowing and is borrowed by physique-focused users.
With less water under the skin, muscle and vascularity look sharper. The look is visible within hours and fades when you rehydrate. It has not been studied as a looksmaxxing method.

paras: Users change water intake and use sauna or sweat-suit sessions over hours to days before the event, then rehydrate afterward.

Sports organisations and emergency physicians have documented serious harm from extreme cuts, including several deaths of combat-sports athletes between 2015 and 2017. Regulators and physicians describe acute water loss as very dangerous, and nutrition experts generally advise against it.

web.title: Peak week recommendations for bodybuilders: an evidence based approach
Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation

chain: Drier, more defined look for a day
angle.text: Losing body water makes skin sit tighter on muscle for a drier, more defined look for a photo or event. The look shows within hours and fades on rehydration.

lead: Water cutting, or a dehydration cut, is the practice of temporarily reducing body water, through water and food manipulation, sweating, sweat suits or saunas, so that the body weighs less or looks drier and more defined. It comes from weight-class sports such as combat sports and rowing, where athletes lose water in the last days before a weigh-in to qualify for a lower class [1]. Physique competitors and people dressing for photos or events use the same idea for looks: the aim is to reduce the water held under the skin so that muscle outlines, veins and the jawline read more sharply.

In bodybuilding the practice is part of what is called peak week, the final days before a show, when competitors manipulate carbohydrate, sodium and water intake in pursuit of a look described as full and dry [2][3]. Reviews describe the stated goal as losing extracellular, subcutaneous water while holding on to water inside the muscle [2]. Surveys of competitors cited in a 2021 review found that water loading followed by restriction was common among natural bodybuilders [2].

Sports regulators, emergency physicians and review authors have documented risks, including deaths of combat-sports athletes between 2015 and 2017 after extreme cuts [1], and case reports of electrolyte disorders in bodybuilders [2]. Reviews of bodybuilding practice state that the effect of dehydration on physique appearance has not been studied [2][3].
infobox: Weight-class sports such as combat sports and rowing [1]

paras: Weight cutting covers two different things: losing fat and muscle over the weeks before an event, and losing water in the last days before competition. The second form is what is popularly called water cutting [1]. Reported methods include restricting food, water loading, and sweating through exercise, a sweat suit or a sauna [1].
Weight is regained afterward by rehydrating and eating, which is why the change is temporary. Combat-sport athletes rehydrate between weigh-in and the bout [1].

A 2021 review by Escalante and colleagues describes body water as split between an intracellular compartment, roughly two thirds, and an extracellular compartment, roughly one third. Physique competitors aim to reduce the subcutaneous part of the extracellular water while preserving the water inside muscle cells [2].

The review cites heat-chamber cycling research in which early water loss was largely extracellular, shifting toward a roughly even split between compartments as dehydration progressed, and the authors suggest that keeping glycogen high may help preserve intracellular water [2]. It also describes work on sodium restriction in which hormonal responses that conserve sodium and water ramp up over about one to two days, a delay the authors suggest could in principle be used to time diuresis [2]. Other approaches the review discusses, such as head-down tilt, are described as producing temporary diuresis that returns to baseline within about 24 hours, with the reviewers noting possible pressure-related downsides at steeper angles [2].

Bodybuilders describe peak week manipulations of carbohydrate, sodium and water as a way to raise muscle glycogen, reduce subcutaneous water and limit bloating. The Escalante review notes that competitors seek to lose extracellular water while preserving intramuscular water [2].

A 2014 review by Helms, Aragon and Fitschen in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition described competitors using fluid and electrolyte manipulation in the final days and hours before a contest to reduce extracellular water and improve size and definition [3].

The 2021 review summarises three studies of what competitors actually do. In a survey of 81 natural bodybuilders, 65.4 percent reported water loading and 32.1 percent water restriction, usually starting 10 to 24 hours before competition, while smaller shares manipulated sodium. In interviews with seven natural bodybuilders, all had water loaded and then cut water, and they described the results as largely ineffective, with three who also manipulated sodium saying they would not do so again. A third study of 382 competitors reported that sodium depletion and dehydration were often used and were described as temporary and necessary despite acknowledged risks [2].

Researchers who have reviewed the topic state that the effect of dehydration and electrolyte manipulation on visual appearance has not been studied [3]. Both reviews note that over-dehydration could produce a flat, depleted look with less muscle fullness, because total body water and muscle water fall together [2][3]. Escalante and colleagues describe a loss of the muscle pump and a withered look as outcomes of going too far, and note that scale weight and its trend can serve as a rough hydration marker [2].

The same review reports that emotional stress can cause fluid retention, with gains of up to 9 kg in 48 hours reported in extreme cases, which is one reason the authors recommend a practice run weeks before an event if any manipulation is used [2].

In December 2015 a 21-year-old Chinese MMA fighter, Yang Jian Bing, died of dehydration while cutting weight for a ONE Championship bout. The promotion then banned dehydration-based cuts, moved to walking-weight arrangements and introduced urine specific gravity testing up to three hours before bouts. Muay Thai fighters Jordan Coe (March 2016) and Jessica Lindsay (November 2017) also died after cutting weight [1]. Emergency physician Paddy Golden described acute water loss as very dangerous and called for hydration testing [1].
In 2022 the Mohegan Tribe Department of Athletic Regulation suspended a fighter for six months and fined him $2,500 after he posted a video of himself vomiting during a cut [1].

For bodybuilding, Escalante and colleagues write that current evidence does not show that water and sodium manipulation is specifically effective or safe. They describe two case reports: a 35-year-old man who developed water intoxication, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, rhabdomyolysis and ECG changes after a week of heavy water intake, a potassium-sparing diuretic and salt restriction before a show, and a 26-year-old professional who developed severe hypokalemia and tachycardia after taking a loop diuretic before a show. Both were treated and discharged [2].

Water intoxication in general is defined as excess water pushing electrolyte balance outside safe limits, with swelling of brain cells; reported symptoms range from headache and confusion to seizures and coma [4]. Nutrition experts rarely give advice on cutting weight and generally recommend against it, according to Wikipedia [1].

No controlled studies have tested dehydration cuts for cosmetic definition. Related research includes a 2019 survey of self-reported weight-cutting methods among professional mixed martial artists [1], a 2013 position statement prepared for the IOC Medical Commission on minimising health risks in weight-sensitive sports [1], and the two peak-week reviews above, which conclude that bodybuilder-specific data on water and sodium manipulation are lacking [2][3]. The 2021 review also describes a study in combat athletes in which several days of water loading followed by restriction produced about 0.6 percent more body-mass loss than in controls [2].

lore.intro: In physique communities the idea circulates mainly as a way to look drier for a shoot or show, and in combat-sport communities as a weigh-in routine. Community claims below reflect that general framing, and the practitioner surveys in the 2021 review give a view of what competitors report.

claims.claim: Dropping water makes you look more shredded for a day
Water cuts are manageable if done briefly
Cutting water while keeping glycogen high keeps the muscles full
Water loading followed by restriction flushes out extra water
